The Greenside darter (Etheostoma blennioides) exhibits a maximum recorded standard length of 13.2 centimeters [Li = 13.2 centimeters] among adults sampled from the Grand River system in Ohio, a value that places it among the larger members of its subgenus. Field surveys indicate that the onset of gonadal recrudescence and subsequent sexual maturation is reached at a remarkably consistent body size; individuals begin developing mature gametes once they attain a standard length of 4.12 centimeters [Lp = 4.12 centimeters]. This early maturation relative to ultimate body size reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes reproductive assurance in an environment where adult mortality can be variable. The relatively modest size at which puberty is achieved allows the species to capitalize on favorable seasonal conditions during its second year of growth, ensuring that a substantial portion of the population is reproductively active during any given spawning season. Comparative data from closely related congeners, such as Etheostoma caeruleum, suggest that this threshold is not phylogenetically fixed but rather shaped by local selective pressures, including the duration of suitable thermal windows for egg incubation and larval development.

Newly emerged prolarvae possess a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.000775 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000775 grams], a value derived from an estimated egg diameter of 1.1 millimeters. This minute initial mass places the yolk-dependent embryo into a critical period of lecithotrophic nutrition following the hatching event, during which the yolk sac is progressively absorbed. The endogenous reserves must sustain the non-feeding larva through the trophic switch until the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding becomes possible, typically occurring a few days after eclosion. The small size of the prolarvae likely renders them vulnerable to a broad suite of planktivorous predators during the brief pelagic phase before they settle into benthic microhabitats. Comparative studies with other darter species that produce larger eggs, such as Etheostoma maculatum, suggest that the relatively reduced investment per offspring in Etheostoma blennioides is compensated for by the production of a correspondingly greater number of oocytes per spawning event, a classic trade-off along the fecundity-egg size continuum.

Mature females can achieve an ultimate wet weight of 27.7 grams [Wwi = 27.7 grams], a body mass that reflects the maximum attainable size under typical conditions found in the species' preferred riffle and run habitats. This asymptotic mass is considerably greater than that reported for smaller-bodied species such as Etheostoma flabellare, underscoring the variation in adult body size that exists within the genus. The attainment of such a mass requires multiple growing seasons and is contingent upon consistent access to benthic macroinvertebrate prey, particularly chironomid larvae and mayfly nymphs. Body condition, often indexed by the residual mass relative to standard length, can fluctuate markedly across seasons, with the highest values recorded in late spring immediately prior to spawning as females accumulate energy reserves for gamete production. The ultimate wet weight also shows modest geographic variation, with populations in more productive stream reaches tending to yield heavier individuals, though the species does not exhibit the pronounced clinal variation seen in some larger percids.

At a sustained water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], female Greenside darters produce approximately 5 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 5 eggs per spawning event] and undertake roughly 1 spawning event per year [F_R_i = roughly 1 spawning event per year], yielding a cumulative annual output of around 5 eggs per year. This rate is achieved by females that spawn repeatedly over an extended breeding season, depositing adhesive eggs in nests guarded by males beneath flat stones or in crevices within gravel substrate. Each reproductive event typically involves the release of a relatively small clutch, but the high frequency of nesting attempts allows for a substantial cumulative seasonal output. Experimental manipulations of photoperiod and temperature indicate that the initiation of breeding activity is tightly coupled to thermal cues, and the rate of gamete production slows markedly when temperatures deviate from the optimal range around 15 °C. This strong thermal dependence of reproductive output has implications for population dynamics under shifting climate regimes, as warmer spring temperatures could advance the onset of spawning and alter the synchronization between larval emergence and peak prey abundance.

The maximum lifespan of the Greenside darter under natural conditions has been estimated at approximately 1,642 days [am = approximately 1,642 days] when maintained at a mean annual water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a longevity that typically spans four to five consecutive breeding seasons. Individuals that recruit successfully into the adult population often survive through their third and fourth years before natural mortality or senescence intervenes. The time from birth to the attainment of puberty is approximately 547 days [tp = approximately 547 days] under these same thermal conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a duration that corresponds to the second spring following the hatching year. This extended maturation period is characteristic of darter species that occupy stable, cool-water habitats where growth rates are moderate but annual survival is relatively high. The post-pubertal reproductive window thus spans roughly two to three years for most individuals, during which iteroparous spawning occurs each spring. Senescence is not abrupt; older females gradually exhibit reduced fecundity and a higher incidence of atretic oocytes, suggesting that reproductive senescence precedes somatic death in this species, a pattern observed in several other iteroparous freshwater teleosts.
